stops.name: Cádiz: la licencia y la partida a Londres
stops.campa: Alvear obtains leave from the army of the King he no longer serves in his heart, and sails from Cádiz for London with Carmen and the commission of lodge number 3: to plant the society at the center of the world. Behind him the Cortes debate liberty for Spain while denying it to America; ahead lies the city of Miranda, of the exiles, of the money and the ships. The canon marks the passage as a change of standard: he leaves as an officer of Spain and lands as an agent of the American nation that does not yet exist.

stops.name: Londres: fundación de la logia n.º 7, por orden de la n.º 3
stops.campa: In London, in the orbit of Miranda's house on Grafton Way, Alvear executes the order of Cádiz: with the brothers San Martín, Zapiola, Chilavert, Villaurrutia and fray Servando Teresa de Mier he founds lodge number 7 of the Caballeros Racionales, its motto unión, firmeza y valor. The lodge is a relay station of the continental revolution: communication with Cádiz, with Philadelphia, with Caracas, and shelter for brothers escaping the peninsula. Around its table sit the man who will free the south of the continent and the friar who will help found Mexico. The oath is taken; the network is complete.

stops.name: Londres: las cartas a Mérida (la voz de la logia)
stops.campa: Alvear writes to his brother Rafael Diego de Mérida of Caracas, reporting the founding of number 7 and the design of the whole web. The letters go aboard the English brig La Rosa bound for Caracas; a Spanish corsair takes her in January, and the lodge's own voice (names, numbers, purposes) passes into the archives of its enemies at Puerto Rico and Madrid. The canon treasures the interception: because of it, the oath of Cádiz and London is not legend but document, preserved forever in the Archivo Álvaro de Bazán by the very empire it condemned.
stops.quote: Aquí he establecido una logia que sirva de comunicación con Cádiz, Filadelfia y esa, así como para dar acogida a los hermanos que escapen de Cádiz.
stops.quote_source: Carta de Alvear a Rafael de Mérida, Londres, 28 de octubre de 1811, interceptada; Archivo General de Marina Álvaro de Bazán

stops.name: Puerto de Londres: a bordo de la fragata George Canning
stops.campa: On 19 January the merchant frigate George Canning drops down the Thames carrying the revolution home. Aboard are Alvear with Carmen, San Martín, Zapiola, Chilavert, the baron Holmberg and a handful of veteran officers of the peninsular war: the whole general staff of a future state traveling as passengers. Their commissions are from no government; their orders are from the lodge. The canon names the ship as the tradition names arks: what the George Canning carries in her cabins is the army, the assembly and the directory of the Provinces to come.

stops.name: Atlántico Sur, a bordo: los cincuenta días
stops.campa: Fifty days of ocean. On the quarterdeck, between the trades and the doldrums, the brothers settle the plan that the next three years will execute point by point: found the lodge in Buenos Aires, take the army, remake the government, convoke the sovereign assembly, carry the war to the Spaniard wherever he stands. Alvear is twenty-two and crossing, in reverse, the same Atlantic that swallowed his mother. The canon reads the voyage as a single held breath between the oath and its fulfillment.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, puerto: desembarco de la George Canning
stops.campa: On 9 March 1812 the George Canning comes to anchor off Buenos Aires and the veterans step ashore into the city of the Revolution of May, now two years old and adrift. The Triumvirate receives them, confirms their ranks, sets San Martín to raising a corps of mounted grenadiers. Alvear, son of a great house, rich, brilliant, twenty-two, moves at once into the center of everything. The Gazeta records an arrival of officers; the canon records the arrival of the instrument that will give the revolution its army and its assembly.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: fundación de la Logia Lautaro
stops.campa: In the months after the landing, Alvear, San Martín and Zapiola found in Buenos Aires the lodge the tradition names Lautaro, after the Araucanian who learned war from his conquerors to destroy them. It is the American filial of Cádiz and London: same oath, same grades, same discipline of secrecy, its members bound to sustain one another in government and war until the continent is free and constituted. The lodge meets, votes, and moves men like columns. From this room the next decade of the Plata is commanded.

stops.name: Plaza de la Victoria: la revolución del 8 de octubre de 1812
stops.campa: At dawn the regiments fill the Plaza de la Victoria (San Martín's grenadiers, Ortiz de Ocampo's men, and Alvear among the chiefs) and the First Triumvirate, worn out and suspected of tepid loyalty to the cause, is set aside by the pressure of the troops and the petition of the people. A Second Triumvirate is sworn, pledged to the lodge's program: a general constituent assembly of the Provinces. Not a shot is fired; the canon counts it a victory of the oath over the government, and the first proof that the brothers of Cádiz now hold the country in their hands.

stops.name: Consulado de Buenos Aires: presidente de la Asamblea del Año XIII
stops.campa: On the morning of 31 January 1813 the deputies hear mass in the Cathedral and march to the Consulado, where the General Constituent Assembly declares that the sovereignty of the people resides in itself, and elects Carlos de Alvear its president by acclamation. He is twenty-three. Under his presidency the Assembly strikes the King's name from the oaths, coins money stamped with the sun, declares free the wombs of slave mothers, abolishes tribute, mita and the instruments of torture, and orders the títulos of nobility burned. The boy of the Misiones presides over the birth certificate of the nation.

stops.name: Líneas del sitio, Cerrito de Montevideo: el mando del ejército
stops.campa: The last royalist stronghold of the Plata has resisted for two years behind its walls. Brown's improvised squadron has just destroyed the Spanish fleet off El Buceo; the sea is closed. Alvear, brigadier general at twenty-four, arrives at the siege lines and takes command of the army before Montevideo, relieving Rondeau. He tightens the trenches, presses the outposts, and opens negotiation with Vigodet while the hungry city counts its biscuit. The canon gives him the quality it gives all its founders in this hour: velocity. Twenty-seven days after he takes the command, the city falls.

stops.name: Montevideo, Portón de San Pedro: la caída de Montevideo
stops.campa: On 22 June the Fortaleza del Cerro is handed over; on the 23rd the keys of the city are delivered and the Spanish garrison files out by the Portón de San Juan as Alvear enters at the head of his escort and staff through the Portón de San Pedro, the Regiment of Pardos y Morenos leading. Seven thousand prisoners, five hundred guns, nine thousand muskets, ninety-nine vessels: the whole apparatus of Spain on the river taken in deposit and never returned. Four years of royalist threat on the Plata end in a morning. He is twenty-four, and this is his first crown of laurel.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: el triunfo y la envidia
stops.campa: Buenos Aires receives the conqueror of Montevideo with arches, salvos and the delirium reserved for the young. The Director Posadas, his own uncle, heaps honors on him; the captured banners hang in the churches. He is the first general of the state at twenty-four, and the canon notes what every canon notes at such altitude: behind the acclamations, envy takes its measurements. The veterans he superseded, the parties he outran, the provinces that fear the capital: all begin, from this day, the slow work of his fall.
